headline: DeepSeek's new Flash model holds a token's key-value cache in 890 bytes of high-bandwidth memory, about a quarter of its predecessor's, by sharing keys across layers and storing them in four-bit floating point.

items.title: Oxygen vacancies at the interlayer, not permittivity, set the memory window
items.dek: Marshall Frye and colleagues at Georgia Tech and Oak Ridge traced the extra memory window that appears when a thin aluminium-oxide layer is stacked inside ferroelectric hafnium–zirconium oxide — the switchable insulator behind hafnia memories — to oxygen vacancies at the interface rather than to the added layer's dielectric constant.
items.why_it_matters: Interlayer stacks have been designed as a capacitor-divider problem: choose a dielectric constant, work out how much of the applied voltage lands on the ferroelectric, predict the window. If the window instead comes from charge tunnelling between defect states at the interface, the design variable becomes the oxygen-vacancy population — an oxidant-dose and anneal parameter you already control — and the same material stack can be retuned without changing materials. It also makes the defects the field has spent fifteen years trying to suppress load-bearing rather than parasitic.
items.background_md: Hafnium oxide interests memory designers because it stays ferroelectric in films a few nanometres thick: alloyed with zirconium it holds a remanent electrical polarisation that flips once the applied field passes a coercive value, and the two stable states are read as a shift in a transistor's threshold voltage. The catch is that the polar orthorhombic phase is metastable and defect-mediated. Oxygen vacancies help stabilise it, and the same vacancies trap charge, drift under field, and eventually kill the device. Every hafnia memory result is therefore an argument about which defects are helping.
items.deeper_md:
The measurements are stacked to close one loop. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with sequential etching finds the interface between HZO and the interlayer is off-stoichiometric, carrying a **2.3× increase in oxygen vacancies**. Polarisation-dependent XPS and first-order reversal curves attribute the shifted coercive fields to tunnelling between those interfacial defect states, giving a bidirectional internal bias of **0.56 MV/cm**. Phase-field modelling then reproduces the coercive fields, the reversal curves and the bias only when defect density and tunnelling barrier height match the measured values, landing on **0.55 MV/cm** — and the fitted model is used to sweep 36 simulated devices over charge density and dielectric thickness.

The price is visible in the neighbouring literature. A silicon-channel FeFET with a 3.4 nm SiO₂ top interlayer reaches a 6.3 V window with ten-year retention, but its authors report endurance falling as the initial window rises. And ozone-dose work on hafnia shows vacancy-rich films cycling to 10⁸ before breakdown against 5 × 10⁹ for a defect-lean film. Engineering vacancies up is engineering lifetime down; this preprint does not report endurance.

glossary.definition: The separation in volts between a ferroelectric transistor's two threshold-voltage states; it has to stay wider than the drift and noise the cell accumulates over its retention period.
The electric field at which a ferroelectric's polarisation reverses. In hafnia it is measured in megavolts per centimetre, so the 0.56 MV/cm internal bias reported here is a shift of comparable size.

A missing oxygen atom in the oxide lattice. It leaves two electrons loosely bound, so it both distorts the local structure that stabilises the polar phase and acts as a charge trap and a leakage path.
A measurement that drives a ferroelectric partway round its hysteresis loop and back, repeatedly, to recover the distribution of switching fields inside the film rather than one averaged loop.

items.fab_angle: The knob this result hands you is an oxidant dose, not a new material — interlayer oxide grown with less oxidant leaves more vacancies at the interface, and the published ozone-dose data show how sharply that trades against cycling life. A lab that can run an atomic-layer deposition recipe can move this variable deliberately instead of discovering it as drift.

items.title: The wiring stack's thermal conductivity turns out to be a layout parameter
items.dek: Zifeng Huang and co-authors measured the thermal conductivity of individual layers inside finished copper interconnect stacks using time-domain thermoreflectance — a pump-probe laser method with roughly 100-nanometre depth resolution — and fitted more than 40 such layer-resolved measurements into an empirical rule that predicts a layer's conductivity from its structure.
items.why_it_matters: Thermal simulation of a stacked chip currently assigns each wiring layer one conductivity taken from a handbook or from a guess, and the hot-spot map it produces inherits that guess. A relation that maps a layer's structure onto its conductivity, together with a model that resolves how conductivity varies across one layer, turns a thermal prediction into something a floorplanner can act on before tapeout rather than a number checked after silicon comes back. It also identifies which layer in the stack is the actual bottleneck instead of assuming the stack is uniform.
items.background_md: A chip's transistors sit underneath ten or more layers of copper wiring separated by low-permittivity insulator, and most of the heat they generate has to leave through that stack or sideways through the substrate. The two materials are thermally opposite: copper carries heat well, the porous organosilicate around it barely at all, and the insulator occupies most of the volume. A wiring layer's effective conductivity is therefore not a material constant. It is a geometry — set by how much metal the layout put in that layer and how the vias between layers line up.
items.deeper_md:
The measurement is the contribution. Time-domain thermoreflectance heats a surface with one ultrafast laser pulse and watches the reflectivity decay with a delayed probe; here it is pushed to roughly **100 nm depth resolution**, which is what makes a single interconnect level separable from the ones above and below it. Statistical analysis of **more than 40 measured layer-resolved conductivities** across differing back-end levels yields a structure-to-conductivity relation, and an intra-layer model built on effective medium theory plus real layouts resolves how that conductivity varies spatially inside one level.

The companion evidence says why structure dominates. Measuring two chips polished down to the M4 and M6 levels, cross-plane thermal resistance follows a simple series model and areal heat capacity scales linearly with metal content; finite-element simulation attributes the limit to the dielectric, because of its volume fraction, with via connectivity a secondary but real effect.

Two caveats. This is a fitted empirical relation over a compiled dataset, not a first-principles prediction, so it extrapolates only as far as the layer types it saw. And reaching a buried level at all meant polishing a finished part down to it.

glossary.definition: Heat flow per unit area divided by temperature gradient. In a composite layer it is an effective value that depends on the volume fractions and the arrangement of the materials, not only on what they are.

A pump-probe optical method: one femtosecond pulse heats the surface, a delayed second pulse measures the reflectivity change, and the decay curve is fitted to a heat-transfer model to extract conductivity and interface resistance.

A way of assigning one transport property to a mixture by averaging over the constituents and their geometry, rather than resolving each copper line — the step that makes a full stack tractable to simulate.

The copper wiring and insulator built above the transistors. It carries every signal and supply on the chip, and its copper and low-k insulator cap the temperature of every process step that comes after it.

items.fab_angle: Dummy metal fill is added to layouts to keep polishing uniform, and this reframes it as a thermal knob as well: metal fraction is what sets a level's effective conductivity, so the fill pattern that satisfies a planarisation density rule is also deciding where heat can leave. The same is true of via farms, which the simulation here scores as a secondary but measurable path.

items.title: Strip the names off the knobs to price what architectural meaning is worth
items.dek: Ambika Sharan, Grigory Chirkov and Soheil Abbasloo handed one language-model agent the same 15-parameter GPU design space twice — once as named architectural knobs with simulator counters, once as anonymous variables between 0 and 1 — and the run that knew what it was tuning found better designs using 70.1 percent fewer simulator calls.
items.why_it_matters: Every published claim that an agent improved a hardware design has varied the agent while holding the framing of the problem fixed, which cannot separate reasoning about a machine from competent black-box search over knobs whose meaning was never recovered — and only the first kind of skill transfers to the next architecture. Holding the evaluator, the legal space and the reachable optima identical and varying only whether the variables mean anything makes the difference measurable. The uncomfortable half is that a critic loop closes most of the gap for the blind agent and buys the informed one nothing.
items.background_md: Designing an accelerator is a search over a discrete space — how many streaming multiprocessors, how much cache at each level, what tile shape the matrix units chew through — in which evaluating a single point means running a simulator, and the simulator is the expensive part. Cycle-accurate models are far too slow at this scale, so architects use analytical simulators that estimate latency and die area from parameters in seconds and accept roughly ten percent error in exchange. Search over that space is old and well understood; what is new is the question of where the search's priors come from.
items.deeper_md:
The 15 dimensions cover streaming-multiprocessor count, tensor-core throughput and the M/N/K dimensions of the matrix tile, L1/L2/L3 capacity and bandwidth, cache-hierarchy depth and domain organisation, register-file tier and L1/L2 fan-out. Memory bandwidth and process node are pinned so the comparison is not smuggling a technology change. The evaluator is an internal simulator derived from LLMCompass, whose published version reports about 10.4 percent mean latency error across operators and 4.1 percent on full LLM inference.

On a nine-kernel FP16 GEMM basket spanning bandwidth-bound decode matrix-vector products through compute-bound matrix multiplies, the named-knob agent beats a modelled H200 by **5.4 percent**, beats its anonymised twin by **12.3 percent** on mean-best latency, and gets there with **70.1 percent fewer simulator calls**.

The authors decline to oversell it: five to six runs per condition, one modelled accelerator, results labelled preliminary, and an explicit worry that the space has broad near-optimal plateaus a blind search can walk onto without understanding anything. A separate group's LUMINA, which composes exploration rules from simulator code, reports six better-than-A100 designs in 20 steps over 4.7 million candidates — a different claim about a different space.

glossary.definition: Searching a parameterised family of hardware designs for the points that best trade performance against area and power, where each evaluation costs a simulator run rather than a closed-form calculation.
The replicated compute block inside a GPU that holds the scheduler, register file, L1 cache and the arithmetic units; counting them is the coarsest knob an architect has.

The three dimensions of the matrix-multiply fragment a tensor core executes in one instruction. The shape decides how much data must be re-fetched per useful multiply, so it couples the arithmetic units to the cache hierarchy.
Useful arithmetic operations per byte moved from memory. It decides whether a kernel is limited by the multipliers or by the memory system, which is why a benchmark basket has to span a range of it.

items.title: Size the checksum against rounding noise, not against hash collisions
items.dek: Pranav Napolean, Vikas Srivastava and Napolean Periathambi built a checker for half-precision matrix multiplication on GPUs that compresses the error with small random matrices instead of redoing the product, and found that the number of buckets it needs is fixed by floating-point rounding noise rather than by the chance of two errors colliding.
items.why_it_matters: Checksum fault tolerance is classically sized from collision probability, which is the right analysis for exact integer arithmetic and the wrong one for a tensor core that accumulates in 32-bit float and hands back 16-bit results. Deriving the bucket count from measured noise instead makes the detector's threshold a calibrated quantity rather than a constant copied out of a paper, and it forces the real cost into the open: on an H100 the probe runs between a quarter and more than twice the time of the multiply it guards.
items.background_md: A GPU tensor core multiplies matrices with no error detection on its accumulators, so a transient upset returns a number that is valid, wrong, and silent. Checksum-based fault tolerance catches this cheaply: multiply both operands by a vector, compare against the same vector applied to the claimed product, and a mismatch means something went wrong — a matrix-vector cost guarding a matrix-matrix one. The awkward part is floating point. The checksum is itself computed in rounded arithmetic, so the alarm threshold must sit above the noise the arithmetic invents and below the smallest fault worth catching.
items.deeper_md:
Detection forms `S = H₁EH₂ᵀ = (H₁A)(BH₂ᵀ) − H₁CH₂ᵀ`, so the error is aggregated into buckets without ever building the full product. Localisation adds first-moment sketches weighted by row and column index; when a bucket holds exactly one error, the ratios of the moment sketches to the sum sketch give back its coordinates. The sizing result is that buckets must grow as **Θ(n^2.57)** for square matrices, with library-dependent constants (0.19 for BF16, 0.33 for FP16 on cuBLAS).

The fault model matters more than the sketching. Injecting at instruction level with NVBit into live FP32 accumulators produces upsets worth only **2 to 9 percent** of a typical output entry — a population that flipping a bit in a finished result cannot generate. Guarding all 32 MLP down-projections of Llama-2-7B removes **99.4 percent** (BF16) and **99.9 percent** (FP16) of the perplexity damage from injected faults.

Cost and limits are stated plainly: probe 0.78–3.06 ms against GEMMs of 0.35–12.47 ms; flipped bit positions are not recoverable under NVBit injection (0 of 80); repair is dearer than simply recomputing.

glossary.definition: Adding checksums to the data an algorithm already computes so that a hardware error shows up as an arithmetic inconsistency, rather than duplicating the whole computation to compare answers.

A hardware fault that changes a result without raising any machine check or exception, so the wrong value propagates through the stack and only surfaces, if ever, as a strange application-level symptom.

Tensor cores take 16-bit operands but sum the partial products in 32-bit floating point before narrowing the result, which is why the rounding noise a checksum must clear depends on both formats at once.
The exponential of a language model's average per-token loss on held-out text. It is the standard sensitivity probe here: a few corrupted entries in one projection move it measurably.

items.title: A counterexample says failure is possible; this says how often
items.dek: Arnab Ray of the Indian Statistical Institute and Aalok Thakkar of Ashoka University combined symbolic execution with adaptive sampling to return a confidence interval on how often a program fails under the input distribution it actually sees, in place of a single counterexample or a yes-or-no proof.
items.why_it_matters: A verifier's verdict is binary and a test's verdict is anecdotal, and neither answers what a reliability requirement asks, which is a rate with an error bar attached. Splitting the input space into a region whose probability mass symbolic execution can compute exactly and a residue bounded statistically yields an interval that provably contains the true failure rate, and it collapses the sampling cost precisely where random testing is worst — on failures too rare ever to be drawn. The cost is that the input distribution must now be written down.
items.background_md: Testing and verification fail the same question from opposite sides. A failing test hands you one input: a defect exists, and nothing follows about how often it is reached. A proof covers every input, including the ones the program will never be given, which is most of why proving industrial code costs what it does. Reliability targets, meanwhile, are stated as rates — failures per demand — and a rate is a joint property of the program and the distribution its inputs are drawn from, which neither method carries anywhere in its machinery.
items.deeper_md:
The framework has three pluggable parts — a mass estimator, a closure rule, and per-leaf confidence bounds — and a decomposition theorem stating that any instantiation satisfying three invariants returns an interval containing the true rate. DiSE instantiates it with SMT-based closure over symbolic paths, variance-adaptive empirical-Bernstein confidence sequences on the remainder, and a scheduler that spends effort by gain per unit cost.

On SV-COMP programs it returns an exact interval on **59 of 126** against 51 for exhaustive refinement, with a median half-width of **0.0030** against 0.043 for pure symbolic execution, and certifies rare events down to ε = 5 × 10⁻³ in constant sample count across four orders of magnitude — up to two orders of magnitude fewer executions than sampling alone.

The scope statement is the honest part, and it is narrow: deterministic programs, finite domains, independent discrete input distributions, Boolean output properties, linear integer arithmetic. Bitwise operators and shifts fall outside the supported fragment, which excludes a great deal of systems code, and the operational distribution is assumed known when estimating it is usually the hard part.

glossary.definition: Running a program with variables in place of concrete inputs, so one run yields a logical formula describing the whole set of inputs that take that path rather than a single result.

A program that decides whether a formula over arithmetic, arrays and bit-vectors can be satisfied and produces a witness if so; here it is what turns a path condition into a region of the input space.
An interval valid at every sample size at once, so you may keep drawing samples and stop when the interval is tight enough without invalidating the guarantee — unlike a fixed-n confidence interval.
The annual International Competition on Software Verification, whose public benchmark set of C programs with known-correct verdicts is the standard yardstick this class of tool is measured against.

items.title: 890 bytes of KV cache per token, and prefill costs half of what decode does
items.dek: DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash, a 552-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model whose causal encoder-decoder layout activates 8 billion parameters while reading a prompt and 16 billion while writing one, and whose per-token key-value cache resident in high-bandwidth memory is down to 890 bytes, roughly a quarter of its predecessor's.
items.why_it_matters: Serving a long-context agent is limited by two different resources at two different moments: reading the prompt is arithmetic over the whole input, writing each token is a sweep of a cache that has grown with every token so far. Activating half as many parameters during the reading phase puts that asymmetry into the architecture instead of leaving it to the scheduler, and a per-token cache figure is what converts an accelerator's memory capacity into a concurrent-session count — which is the number that sizes an inference cluster before any benchmark is run.
items.background_md: A transformer generating text stores, for every token already seen, the key and value vectors of every attention layer, so each new token can attend to the past without recomputing it. That cache sits in the accelerator's high-bandwidth memory, grows linearly with context length, and is read in its entirety to produce each token — so its size governs both how many requests fit on a device and how fast any one of them decodes. Past a certain context length it is memory capacity and memory bandwidth, not arithmetic, that a serving system runs out of first.
items.deeper_md:
The architecture is 40 layers split 20 encoder and 20 decoder, with mixture-of-experts layers holding one shared and 384 routed experts and activating six routed experts per token; the published checkpoint is MIT-licensed and carries 552B backbone parameters, 748B including the Engram components.

The cache figure comes from two stacked tricks. Compressed Sparse Attention 2 assigns each layer one of three static modes — Full, Reindex, Reuse — so that main keys and values and the indexer's keys are shared across layers and top-k index sets are reused rather than recomputed. On top of that the cache is stored in FP4, specifically E2M1 with one E4M3 scale per 16 channels. Together those give **890 bytes per token** resident in HBM. A separate deployment trick, replaying only the most recent window of tokens, cuts the persistent copy on SSD or host memory to about an eighth of the previous generation's.

Everything here is self-reported and the comparisons are against DeepSeek's own V4-Flash, which was 284B parameters with 13B activated. DeepSeek states a remaining gap to larger closed models on science-oriented agentic tasks.

glossary.definition: The stored key and value vectors for every past token at every attention layer. It is what lets a model generate token n+1 without re-reading the first n, and its size grows linearly with context.

A layer holding many parallel feed-forward blocks, of which a router picks a few per token; a shared expert runs for every token. Parameter count grows without the arithmetic per token growing with it.
Field widths of small floats: E2M1 is two exponent bits and one mantissa bit plus sign, a 4-bit number; E4M3 is an 8-bit float used here only as the scale factor shared by a group of 16 channels.
The two phases of generation. Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and is limited by arithmetic; decode emits one token at a time and is limited by how fast the cache can be read.

foundations.subtitle: A lithography tool does not print a pattern; it prints a solubility difference, and the chemistry that turns one into the other has been rebuilt twice.
foundations.tldr: Every exposure tool ever built does the same thing: it delivers a blurry distribution of light onto a polymer film. The film's job is to convert that into a sharp, nearly binary difference in how fast it dissolves in developer. Two chemistries have done this job. The old one spends one photon per molecule and needs a lot of light; the new one spends one photon to trigger hundreds of reactions, which bought deep-ultraviolet lithography and then made the post-exposure bake the most delicate step in the flow.

sections.heading: The image the tool makes is not the image you want
sections.body_md: Start with what arrives at the wafer. A projection lens delivers an aerial image with soft edges — intensity falls off over a distance comparable to the feature itself, and at the smallest pitches the contrast between bright and dark is far from total. Nothing downstream makes that light sharper. What has to happen instead is a conversion: the resist must take a smoothly varying dose and produce a step change in dissolution rate, so that a developer bath removes everything above some threshold and nothing below it. That is the entire job. The number that describes how well a resist does it is contrast, the steepness of the curve relating remaining film thickness to the logarithm of dose, and the dose at which the film first clears completely is called dose-to-clear. A high-contrast resist takes a mediocre aerial image and returns a vertical sidewall; a low-contrast one returns a slope, and the slope becomes the linewidth error.
sections.deeper_md: The conversion is usually described as a threshold model: assume the resist clears wherever the dose exceeds some value, and the printed edge sits where the aerial image crosses it. The useful consequence is that edge placement error equals the image-log-slope divided into the dose error, so every percentage point of dose non-uniformity, and every percentage point of reflectivity variation off the underlying film, lands directly on linewidth. This is why anti-reflective coatings and resist thickness uniformity are treated as lithography problems rather than as coating problems.

sections.heading: Novolac and DNQ: a molecule whose job is to get in the way
sections.body_md: The workhorse chemistry for i-line and g-line exposure is two ingredients and a solvent. The resin is a novolac — cresol and formaldehyde polymerised into a phenolic — and it dissolves readily in aqueous base. On its own that would be useless, because it would dissolve everywhere. The second ingredient, a diazonaphthoquinone, is the switch: mixed into the novolac it hydrogen-bonds to the resin and inhibits dissolution, so the unexposed film barely erodes. Expose it, and the diazonaphthoquinone undergoes a Wolff rearrangement, losing nitrogen and passing through a ketene that picks up water from the film to become an indenecarboxylic acid. That product does not merely stop inhibiting; it actively accelerates dissolution. So the exposed and unexposed regions move apart from both directions at once, which is where the contrast comes from, and the developer is typically a dilute tetramethylammonium hydroxide solution.
sections.deeper_md: Two practical consequences fall straight out of the mechanism. The ketene needs water, which is why a resist film that has been baked too hard or exposed in too dry an ambient develops differently — and why post-exposure delay changes the printed dimension. Work on fluoroalkylated diazonaphthoquinones reports patterns whose thickness and width grow with the delay between exposure and development, exactly the moisture-dependent conversion kinetics the mechanism predicts. The nitrogen released is the second consequence: it outgasses from the film, and in thick resists it can foam.

sections.heading: One photon, one molecule — and what that costs
sections.body_md: Here is the limit built into that chemistry. Each absorbed photon converts at most one sensitiser molecule, so the number of solubility switches you get is bounded by the number of photons you paid for. Doses land in the hundreds of millijoules per square centimetre; measurements on a fluoroalkylated diazonaphthoquinone system, for instance, put patterning at 0.16 J/cm² at 365 nm. That was affordable while the source was a mercury lamp and the feature was half a micrometre. It stopped being affordable at 248 nm, where the available krypton-fluoride laser power was modest and the throughput of a scanner is set by how long each field must sit under the light. The industry needed a resist perhaps a hundred times more sensitive without giving up contrast, and no amount of reformulating a one-photon-one-molecule system was going to supply it.
sections.deeper_md: The sensitivity problem is not only about laser cost. Throughput on a scanner is wafers per hour, and exposure time per field is dose divided by intensity at the wafer; every factor of two in resist sensitivity is, to first order, a factor of two off the exposure component of that time. The same arithmetic is now running again at 13.5 nm, where source power is the single most expensive parameter in the tool and where, awkwardly, the physics pushes in the opposite direction — see the last two sections.

sections.heading: Chemical amplification: the photon stops being the reagent
sections.body_md: The replacement chemistry decouples the two. The resin carries acid-labile protecting groups — commonly tert-butoxycarbonyl or an acetal — that block the sites which would otherwise make the polymer soluble in base. A small amount of photoacid generator is mixed in. Exposure decomposes some of the generator and releases a strong acid, and that is all the light does. The pattern is developed chemically afterwards: during a post-exposure bake the acid attacks a protecting group, cleaves it off, and is regenerated in the process, so it moves on and does it again. The catalytic chain length in a conventional resist runs to a few hundred deprotections per acid molecule. Sensitivity improves by about that factor, which is why reported doses for deep-ultraviolet resists sit in the range of a few to a few tens of millijoules per square centimetre rather than hundreds.
sections.deeper_md: The four-step cascade is worth stating precisely because each step is a separate failure mode: exposure generates acid from the photoacid generator; the bake lets that acid catalyse deprotection of acid-labile groups; the proton is regenerated and continues; development in aqueous base removes the deprotected regions for a positive-tone resist. Published examples span the range — 70 mJ/cm² for 0.35 µm in a thick-film 248 nm resist, 30 mJ/cm² for 0.175 µm in a one-component krypton-fluoride resist, and 2 mJ/cm² at 254 nm with a contrast of 4.2 in a high-sensitivity formulation.

sections.heading: The bake is now the lithography step
sections.body_md: Amplification moves the hardest problem from the exposure tool to a hotplate. The acid has to travel far enough to find protecting groups but not so far that it crosses the line edge, so the printed dimension now depends on a reaction-diffusion process whose extent is set by bake temperature and time. Formulations that tether the generator to the polymer backbone report diffusion lengths held near 50 nm, and base quenchers — usually simple amines mixed into the resist — are added to neutralise stray acid and sharpen the boundary between exposed and unexposed regions. The failure this invites is famous: airborne base drifting through the fab air neutralises acid at the top surface of the film before the bake can use it. That surface then fails to deprotect, resists development, and the printed line acquires a flared head. It is called T-topping, and it is why chemically amplified resists live in filtered air and on a clock.
sections.deeper_md: The quencher does two jobs that are easy to conflate. It raises the effective threshold, discarding the low-level acid generated in nominally dark regions by flare and by the tail of the aerial image, which improves contrast. And it shortens the acid's effective diffusion length by removing molecules that wander, which improves resolution. Both cost sensitivity, because some of the acid you paid photons for is destroyed on purpose. That three-way pull — resolution against line-edge roughness against sensitivity — is the trade every resist formulation is a point on.

sections.heading: Where amplification runs out: counting molecules at 13.5 nm
sections.body_md: At extreme ultraviolet the same dose is delivered by far fewer photons, because each one carries much more energy. Counting stops being a formality. A coarse-grained simulation of a 32 × 32 × 30 nanometre resist volume works with on the order of 1,200 absorbed photons, generating acid at a quantum yield of two per photon and letting it diffuse with a coefficient of 0.2 nm²/s. The roughness that comes out is not small: line-edge roughness between 3.2 and 4.1 nanometres at a 34 mJ/cm² dose, falling to between 1.38 and 3.35 nanometres at 50 mJ/cm². And photons are not the only random variable — the same study finds that changing only the initial polymer chain conformations, with the photon distribution held fixed, shifts roughness by 0.8 to 1.36 nanometres, against 1.06 to 3.22 nanometres from changing the photon pattern alone. The polymer itself is a source of noise.
sections.deeper_md: This is why the current research direction is to stop amplifying and start absorbing. Metal-oxide resists put a heavy element in the molecule: tin-based compounds are reported with absorption coefficients two to three times those of conventional organic chemically amplified resists, so fewer of the scarce photons pass through unused, and the imaging mechanism does not depend on a catalytic chain that blurs. Reported performance is genuinely competitive — zinc-based resists printing 22 to 50 nm half-pitch dense lines at around 20 mJ/cm², and zirconium oxo clusters with a threshold dose near 3 mJ/cm² and a dose-to-full-height near 13 mJ/cm². What they give up is thirty years of process knowledge about how to spin, bake, develop and strip an organic polymer.

glossary.definition: A phenolic resin made by acid-catalysed polymerisation of cresol with formaldehyde. Its phenol groups are what make it soluble in aqueous base, which is the property the sensitiser exists to switch off.

The photosensitive dissolution inhibitor in i-line resists. Unexposed it hydrogen-bonds to the resin and slows dissolution; exposed it rearranges to a carboxylic acid that speeds dissolution up, so the two regions separate from both ends.
A compound that releases a strong acid when it absorbs light. In a chemically amplified resist it is the only thing the exposure actually does; everything after it is catalysis during the bake.

A chemical group — tert-butoxycarbonyl, an acetal — bonded to the polymer to block the site that would make it dissolve in base. Acid cleaves it off and is regenerated, which is what makes the reaction catalytic.

The hotplate step after exposure during which the photogenerated acid diffuses and deprotects. Because the printed dimension depends on how far the acid travels, its temperature and time are lithography parameters, not housekeeping.

A base, usually an amine, added to the resist to neutralise acid that strays out of the exposed region. It buys resolution and contrast by destroying some of the acid the exposure paid for, so it always costs sensitivity.

Contrast is the slope of remaining film thickness against the logarithm of dose; dose-to-clear is the dose at which a positive resist first clears to the substrate. Together they describe how binary the resist's response is.

The random wiggle of a printed edge, and of a line's width, measured as a standard deviation in nanometres. At extreme ultraviolet it is dominated by how few photons and how few molecules are involved per edge.

foundations.try_this: Measure a contrast curve on the resist that is already on the club's shelf, using the maskless stepper as the exposure source. Coat and soft-bake a set of identical wafers or coupons, expose each to a different dose spanning perhaps a factor of twenty, develop them all together for the same time in the same fresh developer, and measure remaining thickness with the profilometer. Plot normalised thickness against the logarithm of dose: the dose where the line hits zero is D₀, and the slope through the transition is γ. Two things make this worth a Saturday rather than an afternoon. First, develop them together — developer temperature and age move D₀ enough to swamp the effect you are looking for. Second, repeat one dose point after letting the exposed coupon sit for an hour before developing. If the resist is a DNQ type the delay should barely register; if the delay moves the edge, you have measured the moisture and diffusion sensitivity the mechanism above predicts, on your own bench.
